stories.headline: IRAN STRIKES TWO OIL TANKERS IN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ, PUSHING WTI CRUDE PAST $86 AND UP MORE THAN 20% FOR THE MONTH
stories.body: Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Friday it struck two tankers operating under U.S. military escort as they tried to transit the Strait of Hormuz, forcing four other vessels to reverse course; WTI crude jumped about 3.5% to $86.80 a barrel, extending July's gain past 20% as traders price in disruption risk to a route carrying roughly a quarter of the world's seaborne oil.
stories.explain: The Strait of Hormuz is the only maritime exit from the Persian Gulf, so a credible threat to tanker traffic forces oil prices to move immediately on the risk of disrupted supply, well before any barrels actually stop flowing, because shippers and insurers reroute or pause transit rather than gamble on a vessel getting hit. That risk premium gets embedded directly into crude, and because oil feeds both headline CPI and the transport cost of nearly every other good, a 20%-plus monthly move complicates the Fed's inflation fight at the exact moment it's already debating a hike. Watch the WTI-Brent spread: a widening gap signals traders see the disruption risk concentrated in U.S.-bound Gulf grades rather than the broader global market.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD JUMPS TO 4.74%, ITS HIGHEST SINCE EARLY 2025, AS FED OFFICIALS SAY A HIKE IS NEEDED
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose roughly 7 basis points to 4.74% Friday after several Fed officials said publicly they now favor raising rates to get ahead of inflation, two days after the committee held rates steady in a 9-3 vote with three dissents favoring a hike; futures markets are pricing more than a 70% chance of a 25-basis-point hike in September, up from roughly 50% a week ago.
stories.explain: This is the bond market repricing the Fed's path through both the expected-rate and term-premium channels at once: rising hike odds lift near-term yields as investors demand compensation for holding fixed-rate debt into a higher-rate world, and that repricing propagates out to the 10-year as the whole curve adjusts. Officials saying this out loud right after a contested hold is a more forward-looking signal than the vote itself, which is why markets moved on it immediately. With oil now driving inflation expectations higher at the same time, the Fed faces a classic supply-shock dilemma: hiking to fight energy-driven inflation risks slowing growth further, since raising the fed funds rate does nothing to add oil supply.

stories.headline: S&P 500 CLOSES A VOLATILE JULY WITH A 0.7% GAIN AS AMAZON'S RECORD QUARTER OFFSETS A DECLINE IN APPLE
stories.body: Amazon reported revenue of $200.6 billion, up nearly 20% year-over-year, with AWS growing to $42.2 billion at a 39.4% operating margin, while Apple posted its strongest June quarter ever at $109.4 billion in revenue but still fell 1.4% to $333.43 after investors flagged that roughly $0.11 of the EPS beat came from one-time tariff refunds rather than core growth; the S&P 500 added 0.7% to close near 7,490 and the Nasdaq 100 rose about 1% to roughly 28,390.
stories.explain: Wall Street is pricing the quality of earnings, not just the headline beat: AWS's 39% operating margin shows Amazon converting cloud revenue into free cash flow at a rate that funds its own AI capex without diluting shareholders, the same self-funding-growth story that moved Microsoft's stock earlier this week, while Apple's tariff-refund boost is a non-recurring item that mechanically won't repeat next quarter, making the underlying growth rate thinner than the headline number suggests. This is the second earnings pair this week where similar-sized beats produced opposite stock reactions purely on capital-allocation credibility. Because a handful of mega-caps carry outsized index weight, one name's quality miss can offset even a genuinely strong beat like Amazon's at the index level.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS TO ROUGHLY $4,086 AS A FIRMER DOLLAR OFFSETS SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND FROM THE HORMUZ ESCALATION
stories.body: Gold eased about 0.3% to roughly $4,086 an ounce even as tensions in the Strait of Hormuz escalated, as the dollar index climbed to 100.12 on rising rate-hike odds and offset the haven bid; the metal remains up more than 2% for July and on pace for its first monthly gain in five months.
stories.explain: Gold is caught between two forces pulling in opposite directions today: rising Fed-hike odds and a firmer dollar raise the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset and make it pricier for foreign buyers, while the Hormuz escalation is exactly the kind of geopolitical shock that normally pushes haven demand higher regardless of rates. When those forces roughly offset, as they did today, the net move tells you which one is dominating at the margin - here, the rates and dollar channel won out. It's a reminder that gold rarely trades on one clean catalyst; a sudden worsening of the Hormuz standoff, like an actual tanker sinking, could flip that balance quickly.

stories.headline: OHIO JUDGE GRANTS INJUNCTION FORCING THE NCAA TO GRANDFATHER 24 MEN'S AND WOMEN'S BASKETBALL PLAYERS INTO FIFTH-YEAR ELIGIBILITY
stories.body: A federal judge in Ohio granted a preliminary injunction allowing 24 players from the high school class of 2022, previously denied a fifth season under the NCAA's new age-based eligibility model, to compete this year, ruling the exclusion 'arbitrary and capricious' and citing irreparable harm from losing a shot at March Madness exposure; the NCAA must post a $200,000 bond as the case proceeds to discovery, with a separate Colorado lawsuit expected to resolve within the week.

stories.headline: GRIZZLIES SEND JA MORANT TO THE TRAIL BLAZERS FOR JERAMI GRANT AND KRIS MURRAY, COMPLETING MEMPHIS'S TEARDOWN OF ITS FORMER CORE
stories.body: Memphis traded two-time All-Star Ja Morant to Portland for forwards Jerami Grant and Kris Murray plus $1 million cash, marking the third and final departure from the Grizzlies' former franchise trio after Desmond Bane and Jaren Jackson Jr. were also moved this offseason; Morant, who has played just 79 games over the last three seasons because of injuries and off-court issues, remains under contract through 2027-28.

stories.headline: DEEBO SAMUEL RETURNS TO THE 49ERS AFTER ONE SEASON IN WASHINGTON AS TRAINING CAMP HOLDOUTS AND EXTENSIONS PILE UP LEAGUE-WIDE
stories.body: San Francisco reacquired wide receiver Deebo Samuel a year after trading him to the Commanders, while New Orleans locked up Chris Olave on a four-year, $132 million extension and Tampa Bay's Baker Mayfield publicly aired frustration after the Buccaneers declined to extend him, leaving him to play the 2026 season on an expiring deal.

stories.headline: SENATE ADJOURNS WITHOUT VOTING ON THE PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT AS UNC PLACES FOOTBALL GM MICHAEL LOMBARDI ON LEAVE
stories.body: The U.S. Senate left for recess Friday without scheduling a vote on the Protect College Sports Act, leaving college football's NIL and revenue-sharing framework unresolved heading into the season, while North Carolina placed general manager Michael Lombardi on paid administrative leave amid an ongoing program review; Indiana's Curt Cignetti, fresh off last season's national title, continued to draw SEC interest at Big Ten Media Days.

sports.detail: Head coach Jedd Fisch will call plays himself for a third straight season after offensive coordinator Jimmie Dougherty parted ways with the program in February. Washington opens Big Ten play against Minnesota on Sept. 26 - the programs' first meeting since 1977 - and hosts reigning champion Indiana later in the year. The Huskies open the season Sept. 5 at home against Washington State in the Apple Cup.

The full roster has arrived on Montlake, with commit Wini Braga working out alongside center Lathan Sommerville. Season tickets for Washington's third Big Ten season went on sale this week, with a home slate against Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Oregon and UCLA plus a neutral-site game against Baylor on Dec. 19 at Climate Pledge Arena.

Seattle held its first padded practice of training camp Thursday, and rookie nose tackle Deven Eastern, sidelined for most of the offseason program, returned to the field off the PUP list. The defending Super Bowl champions open the regular season Sept. 9 against New England in the NFL's Kickoff Game.

Restricted free agent Jalen Duren is reportedly weighing signing his one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer as talks on a long-term deal stretch toward August, with Duren seeking a five-year, $287 million-plus extension that Detroit hasn't matched. The Pistons are also integrating John Collins, Taurean Prince and Gary Harris after last week's 10-player, six-team deal sent out Isaiah Stewart, Caris LeVert and Marcus Sasser.

The Dodgers closed out the series Thursday behind a Dalton Rushing three-run homer and a Teoscar Hernandez solo shot in a 6-2 win. The Mariners wrap their road trip in Los Angeles and turn to the next stop on the schedule.

Strait of Hormuz tensions — watch for further IRGC action against tankers and any U.S. military response

deepDive.title: Why an Oil Shock Is the Fed's Hardest Problem: Supply-Side Inflation and the Limits of Rate Policy
content: Today's brief has one thread running through nearly every story: crude oil above $86 a barrel, up more than 20% for the month, after Iran struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. That single input is doing a lot of work - it's a big reason the 10-year yield jumped to 4.74%, why Fed officials are now openly talking about a hike, and part of why gold's safe-haven bid is fighting a firmer dollar to a draw. For a finance student, this is a clean case study in why supply-side inflation shocks are uniquely difficult for a central bank to manage, in a way that demand-side inflation simply isn't.

Oil enters inflation data two ways: directly, through the energy component of CPI, which typically carries a weight in the high single digits, and indirectly, through transportation and production costs embedded in nearly everything else - a trucking company's diesel bill, an airline's jet fuel, a factory's input costs. The direct effect shows up within weeks; the indirect, cost-push effect propagates through supply chains over months, which is why economists distinguish headline CPI (which captures the immediate energy spike) from core CPI (which strips out food and energy to gauge whether the shock is becoming embedded in underlying prices). The Fed cares deeply about that distinction because it determines whether the shock is temporary or self-reinforcing.

What most people miss is that raising interest rates doesn't put a single additional barrel of oil into the market - it works entirely by suppressing demand elsewhere in the economy, for things like housing, autos and business investment, to make room in the price index for the involuntary spending on gasoline and heating. That's the essence of a supply shock's stagflationary bite, first understood clearly during the 1973 OPEC embargo, when the Fed under Arthur Burns hesitated to tighten aggressively and let inflation expectations become unanchored, a mistake Paul Volcker spent the early 1980s reversing with rates above 15% and a deep recession. Central banks have studied that episode closely ever since precisely because it shows how costly it is to let a supply shock convince the public that inflation is now structural rather than transitory.

That history is exactly why Fed officials are talking about a hike today rather than waiting: with CME FedWatch pricing over a 70% chance of a September move, the committee appears to be trying to get ahead of the psychological tipping point where an oil-driven headline number starts shaping wage and pricing decisions across the economy, rather than repeat the 1970s pattern of chasing inflation after it's already embedded. The risk they're weighing is real - hiking into an oil shock also slows the parts of the economy that had nothing to do with Hormuz - which is why the next few inflation prints, and whether the Strait of Hormuz standoff de-escalates or worsens, will matter more for markets than almost anything else on the calendar.
